decisions.quote:
Our application of his methods to more recent data shows that the results that
              Amihud identified in his analyses are time-dependent. We find that illiquidity
              appears to have been priced in the cross-section during the later period, but its
              relation to asset prices is much less strong than in the earlier period. The time-
              series results show that only unexpected illiquidity is related to index returns
              in the latter period whereas Amihud finds that both unexpected and expected
              illiquidity are related in the earlier period.
decisions.reason: The shipped quote only describes the reconstruction of the original 1963–1997 sample period. In the out-of-sample replication on 1998–2015 data, the cross-sectional and unexpected-illiquidity effects hold in weakened form, whereas the expected-illiquidity time-series effect fails to replicate, which the authors explicitly contrast with Amihud (2002).

shipped.title_o: Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects
shipped.outcome_quote: Using the current version of the CRSP dataset, we obtain essentially the same results that Amihud presents.

blind_target.title: Illiquidity and Stock Returns: Cross-Section and Time-Series Effects.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
This study replicates and updates Amihud’s (2002) seminal paper “Illiquidity
             and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects,” which is among the most
             cited papers in asset pricing, both by academics and practitioners.1
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Our application of his methods to more recent data shows that the results that
              Amihud identified in his analyses are time-dependent. We find that illiquidity
              appears to have been priced in the cross-section during the later period, but its
              relation to asset prices is much less strong than in the earlier period. The time-
              series results show that only unexpected illiquidity is related to index returns
              in the latter period whereas Amihud finds that both unexpected and expected
              illiquidity are related in the earlier period.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: New-period cross-sectional illiquidity pricing remains supported, while the expected-illiquidity time-series effect is absent and only unexpected illiquidity remains related. This explicit contrast, rather than reduced effect size alone, supports mixed. Original-period reconstruction also succeeds.
